tips: To say "I'm vegetarian" in Cantonese, say 我食齋 (ngoh sik jaai); it helps to show the characters on your phone, since Chinese vegetarian restaurants are often called 齋 (jaai) or 素食 (so sik) places.

Plain-looking Cantonese vegetables and noodles are often cooked with oyster sauce (蠔油), chicken or pork stock (上湯), fish sauce, dried shrimp or shrimp paste, so ask for 唔要蠔油 (m yiu hoh yau, "no oyster sauce") and check what the broth is made from.

In ordinary dim sum restaurants, har gow and siu mai contain shrimp or pork, and many pastries (such as egg tarts and flaky buns) can be made with lard, so dedicated vegetarian dim sum places like Lock Cha are the safest choice.

Chinese Buddhist vegetarian (齋) cooking avoids meat and fish, and often also egg, garlic and onion, but dairy and egg are not always excluded, so vegans should say 唔要蛋，唔要奶 (m yiu daan, m yiu naai, "no egg, no milk").
Mock meat in Chinese vegetarian restaurants is made from soy, wheat gluten or mushroom, so the "goose", "char siu" or "fish" on the menu is meat-free, but people avoiding gluten should take care.

Tofu pudding (豆腐花, dau fu fa) with ginger or sugar syrup is a widely available local dessert that is usually vegan, while many other Hong Kong desserts, such as mango sago and milk tea, contain dairy.

Use HappyCow to find vegan and vegetarian places, and OpenRice (Hong Kong's main restaurant review app, in English) to check reviews, opening hours and recent closures before you go, because restaurants in Hong Kong open and close often.
